```{r setup}

# Packages
if (!require("pacman")) install.packages("pacman")
pacman::p_load(tidyverse,
               palmerpenguins,
               gapminder,
               gt,
               scales,
               ggthemes)

# Brand palette — mirrors the variables defined in dataviz-best-practices.scss.
# (R can't read SCSS, so this is the one place hex values are repeated.)
brand <- list(
  bg        = "#F9EBDC",
  primary   = "#317168",
  secondary = "#9D792F",
  accent    = "#F1655F",
  dark      = "#292F20",
  muted     = "#94a3b8",
  gratuitous = "#725496"  # deliberately off-brand, for the "before" examples
)

```

```{r data}

# Time-series data: monthly data from the economics dataset
df_unemployment <- economics |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2009-01-01"), date <= as.Date("2009-12-01"))

# Summary table data: gapminder, 2007 snapshot by continent
df_continents <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(
    countries    = n(),
    mean_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp),
    total_pop    = sum(as.numeric(pop))
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_pop))

```

# Why do we have slides in a talk? {background-color="var(--divider-bg)"}

::: {.notes}
"Highest Level Situation"

Verbally: a good place to start is being clear on why we have slides in a talk
in the first place…
:::

:::

[The talk]{.emphasis} drives impact.
:::

::: {.fragment .slide-body-heading}
Slides simply [reinforce the talk]{.emphasis}.

:::

::: {.notes}
Slides are not where a talk starts.

Verbally: Don't worry! We WILL talk about slides. We just want to be clear that
slides are not where a talk starts.
:::

## Ask: What can the slides do better than my words?

- **Keep the audience's attention** — the talk is bound by time and attention
- **Understand and care about the information** — by directly reinforcing what the speaker is saying
- **Remember it** — dual-encoding with multiple senses (hearing *and* seeing); brain science backs up that using multiple senses aids retention


## What slides should not (primarily) do

- Remind the speaker what they're supposed to be saying

. . .

*Caveat: break in case of emergency… they **can** be a visual aid to keep the speaker on track; that's just a natural artifact if they do their primary job well!*


# Most slide decks fail to deliver {background-color="var(--divider-bg)"}

::: {.notes}
"The Challenge"

Verbal: this is partly because we don't stop and think about what the role of
the slides is, but it's also because we operate as though the brain easily does
some things that it just doesn't. We're going to briefly dip into some light
neuroscience here…
:::

## Maximize the data-pixel ratio!

<br><br>

::: {.ratio-fraction}
::: {.ratio-annotation}
Pixels that represent actual data or information
:::
::: {.numerator}
Data-Information Pixels
:::

All Non-Background Pixels
:::

Every pixel that is not simply the background color
:::
:::

<br>

[Tufte posited "the data-ink ratio"; Stephen Few derived "the data-pixel ratio."]{.muted}

::: {.notes}
Visually define — multiple slides, but they go quick.

Close with, verbally: this is reducing cognitive load by giving the brain fewer
decisions to make about "what matters."
:::


## (Increase the data-pixel ratio of) A chart {visibility="uncounted"}

:::{style="position: relative; width: 75%; margin: 0 auto;"}

```{r chart-default}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center
#| out.width: 90%

gg <- ggplot(df_unemployment, aes(x = date, y = unemploy, color = "unemploy")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("unemploy" = brand$gratuitous)) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "1 month") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_comma(),
    limits = c(0, ceiling(max(df_unemployment$unemploy) / 20000) * 20000),
    breaks = seq(0, ceiling(max(df_unemployment$unemploy) / 20000) * 20000, by = 20000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title  = "Unemployed Persons by Month in 2009",
    x      = "Month",
    y      = "000s of Unemployed Persons",
    color  = NULL
  ) +
  # worsen things up a bit by adding a gratuitous legend and plot border
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.background  = element_rect(linewidth = 0.75, color = "gray40", fill = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(10,10,10,10,"pt")
  )

gg

```

[&larr; Ignore]{.callout-label .absolute .fragment top="30%" left="95%" fragment-index=1}
[Ignore &rarr;]{.callout-label .absolute .fragment top="3%" left="18%" fragment-index=2}
[Tilt my head to read! &rarr;]{.callout-label .absolute .fragment top="45%" left="-18%" fragment-index=3}
[&uarr; Tilt my head to read!]{.callout-label .absolute .fragment top="95%" left="55%" fragment-index=4}
[&uarr; I already knew that]{.callout-label .absolute .fragment top="99%" left="38%" fragment-index=5}

:::

::: {.notes}
Quick hit: before / after. These all can be literally a quick hit
before/after; can return to that to go deeper as to what's going on.

Each callout is a click, building up the cognitive load the audience is
carrying while reading a "default" chart.
:::


## (Increase the data-pixel ratio of) A chart {visibility="uncounted"}

:::{style="position: relative; width: 75%; margin: 0 auto;"}

```{r higher-data-pixel}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center
#| out.width: 90%

gg <- ggplot(df_unemployment, aes(x = date, y = unemploy, color = "unemploy")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("unemploy" = brand$primary)) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "1 month") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_comma(),
    limits = c(0, ceiling(max(df_unemployment$unemploy) / 20000) * 20000),
    breaks = seq(0, ceiling(max(df_unemployment$unemploy) / 20000) * 20000, by = 20000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title  = "Unemployed Persons (000s) by Month in 2009",
    color  = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = brand$bg, color = NA),
    axis.title = element_blank()
  )

gg
```

:::

::: {.notes}
The "after": same data, higher data-pixel ratio. No border, no legend, no
redundant axis titles, horizontal month labels.
:::


## (Increase the data-pixel ratio of) A table

```{r table-before}

# The "before": default-ish gt table with heavy fills, borders, and banding
df_continents |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    continent    = "Continent",
    countries    = "Countries",
    mean_lifeExp = "Mean Life Expectancy",
    total_pop    = "Total Population"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = mean_lifeExp, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(columns = total_pop, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(34),
    column_labels.background.color = brand$gratuitous,
    row.striping.include_table_body = TRUE,
    table_body.hlines.width = px(2),
    table_body.vlines.width = px(2),
    table_body.vlines.style = "solid",
    table.border.top.width = px(3),
    table.border.bottom.width = px(3)
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()

```

::: {.notes}
Quick hit: before / after…
:::


## (Increase the data-pixel ratio of) A table {visibility="uncounted"}

```{r table-after}

# The "after": same data, minimal ink — light rules only where they aid scanning
df_continents |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    continent    = "Continent",
    countries    = "Countries",
    mean_lifeExp = "Mean Life Expectancy",
    total_pop    = "Total Population"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = mean_lifeExp, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(columns = total_pop, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(34),
    table.background.color = brand$bg,
    column_labels.border.bottom.width = px(2),
    column_labels.border.bottom.color = brand$dark,
    column_labels.border.top.style = "hidden",
    table_body.hlines.style = "hidden",
    table.border.bottom.style = "hidden"
  )

```

## (Increase the data-pixel ratio of) Code!

```{r code-before}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000,
         species = as.factor(species),
         island = as.factor(island),
         sex = as.factor(sex))

model_spec <- lm(body_mass_kg ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm +
                   bill_depth_mm + species + sex,
                 data = penguins_clean)

model_summary <- broom::tidy(model_spec, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)

model_summary |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
```

::: {.notes}
Quick hit: before / after — limit the initial version to JUST be reducing the
volume of code shown and making ONE LINE of the code a larger font and
bold/black; other code is "context" — smaller font BUT NOT SMALL and lighter
color BUT NOT TOO LIGHT such that there is projector risk.

[Placeholder styling note: the "after" treatment below uses Quarto's
code-line-numbers highlighting; a fuller size/color treatment may need SCSS
tuning against the syntax highlighter.]
:::


## (Increase the data-pixel ratio of) Code! {visibility="uncounted"}

```{r code-after}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "4"

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)

model_spec <- lm(body_mass_kg ~ flipper_length_mm + species + sex,
                 data = penguins_clean)
```


## Building information (Make it impossible to ignore)

```{r code-build}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-2|4-5|4"

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)

model_spec <- lm(body_mass_kg ~ flipper_length_mm + species + sex,
                 data = penguins_clean)
```

Choose a template that represents you (avoid the default)

::: {.notes}
Pushes the same code example farther with builds and even a highlight: each
click walks through the code, ending with the key line highlighted alone.
:::


## "Brain breaks" can be useful

Brain breaks (Make it interesting to pay attention):

- **Reveal** — show something that is hard to describe (often a moment of revelation)
- **Explain** — images can create connections that words cannot
- **Delight** — aesthetics keep people interested

<br>

Gifs, comics, memes, blank screen

::: {.notes}
For the audience (TED book).
:::
